en: A Case Study of Romantasy: The Cruel Prince
A Case Study of Romantasy: The Cruel Prince

body.value: The animation of the map immediately helps the audience to understand that they are entering a different world. In the book, the story begins before they enter the new world, and they go through a portal to enter Faerieland. A significant amount of time passes between them entering Faerie and the main storyline beginning. The creators of the film elected to skip the introduction of the story, and skip straight to Jude's existence in Faerie.

The animated introduction is also deisgned to show the audience that this story takes place in a secondary world. It also acts as foresahdowing, because each scene of the animation is based on something that happens within the text.
Despite the story taking place in a realm called Faerie, the story is not a fairytale. It is a much darker story, closer to the mythology of faeries from Ireland.

The rules of the fantasy world Jude has found herself in are that everyone is on their own, and anyone can betray anyone. It becomes clear very quickly that Jude's main focus is the survival of herself and her family.

This scene helps define the society they live in. Madoc acts as Jude's guardian, and Jude must obey Madoc's orders. The reference to standing up to Cardan also begins to establish that they are from different classes, and Cardan has more control over the world they live in than Jude does.

The close-up of Jude's hand reveals the rowan berries she wears on a bracelet. These prevent faeries from being able to control her using a glamour. As long as she wears the rowan berries, her free will is protected.

Jude's determination to avoid the classes where she is reminded of her place hint towards her aspirations to more. She intends to become a knight, because that is the only way humans are able to gain power in Faerie, and it is the only path to power she will accept.

After kicking the dirt into Jude's face and fruit, Nicasia implies that she is from dirt, and to dirt she will return. This is further setting up Jude's place in society. She is considered dirt to the Faeries, who are immortal, and she will eventually die, and be buried in dirt. The Fae have little regard for mortals.

This scene explores the barrier between Jude and Cardan. Cardan uses his status to try to force people to his will, and Jude refuses to bow to Cardan's status, and even hits him, which could end badly for her later.

Jude carries salt because salt can be used to break enchantments. It is not toxic to faeries, all it does it make their fruit taste disgusting. The simple act of rebellion is enough to draw Cardan's ire to Jude.

The conversation between Jude and Taryn further defines the society they live in. Cardan's royal status provides him a certain level of immunity for any retaliations he makes. Jude doesn't have the same protections because she's a mortal. She has no real power, and no real control.

Jude and Taryn are able to protect themselves from Faerie glamours, but they cannot defend themselves against a non-magical attack, especially one that they don't see coming. Jude has been training to become a knight, but she dropped her knife, the only weapon she had to defend herself. Without her knife, she is unable to protect herself or her sister. Being defenceless makes her feel weak, which is why the barrier exists between her and Cardan. He is never as defenceless as her.

The Faeries have little regard for the frailty of mortals, and the way Nicasia speaks about mortals makes it clear that she believes they can be easily replaced. There are plenty more mortals. Nicasia believes the value of the Fae to be much higher. It reinforces the barrier between Jude and Cardan because Cardan is used to having to demand attention and respect. If he allows his friends to know that he cares for Jude at all, it will weaken his image in their eyes.

Jude is only willing to betray her own ideals when one of her family members is in danger. She would tell Cardan whatever he wanted to hear as long as it would save her sister. Jude doesn't care if her actions get her killed, but she would never forgive herself if something happened to Taryn because of her. It is her stubbornness and steadfastness that draws Cardan's attention to her. The way she refuses to allow him the upper hand, even when he definitely has it.

Cardan is isolating Jude here, further enforcing the barrier between them, by ensuring her sister can no longer help her. However, in Cardan's eyes, he is doing Jude a favour. He is protecting her sister from the wrath of his friends, ensuring their ire will only be directed towards Jude. This is a moment, later, that will remind Jude of the fact that Cardan did what he could to protect her family, even when he couldn't help her directly.

If Jude would surrender, Cardan could convince his friends to leave her alone. He never intended to put her in harm's way, but he knew his friends would not stop tormenting her, until she surrendered. If she would simply stop resisting, he could try to protect her, but Jude refuses to surrender. It is part of what draws Cardan to her. He is used to having people bow to him simply because of his title. Jude's resistance is unusual to him, and he doesn't understand why she does it.

Cardan is attempting to warn Jude, to remind her that she is mortal, that she cannot face them and win. Jude is determined to find a way anyway. She will prove him wrong, one way or another. She will continue to draw Cardan's attention, and his ire.

Jude's determination to win revenge over Cardan cements the barrier between them. As long as she resists Cardan, he has to antagonise her. As long as he is the one leading the attacks, he can control how badly Jude is hurt. If he stops attacking her, the attacks from his friends will be much more cruel, and much more devastating to Jude.

Taryn saying "they're just words to us" is a reference to the rules of Faerie. Faeries cannot lie, but humans can. The only power Jude really has is the ability to lie without consequence. Faeries are kept to their oaths much more easily than humans.

Cardan's sword pointing at Jude is symbolic of his choice to target Jude during this tournament. It is a threat and a last warning. If she fails to leave the tournament, he will not be responsible for his actions.

They are very evenly matched in terms of sworplay, and part of Jude's determination in this scene is to take Cardan down. If she can prove herself against a Prince of Faerie, she will have respect and renown that she could not earn otherwise. Her intention to humiliate Cardan further implements the barrier between Cardan and Jude.
Cardan baited Jude with her sister, which draws out Jude's anger. Instead of remembering strategy, she only remembers her rage.
Cardan baited Jude with her sister, which draws out Jude's anger. Instead of remembering strategy, she only remembers her rage.
Jude embarasses Cardan in front of his friends and his family. The tournament makes him look bad, because he was bested by a mortal. She beat a Faerie in battle, and earned herself renown.

Cardan seeks his revenge, reminding Jude that the little power she's won can be taken away as easily as her life. Cardan's constant threats towards Jude also create the barrier between them, but they also add to Jude's attraction to Cardan. She can't resist proving him wrong. She is determined to best him. She plans everything so that he will be the one under her control, which will eventually lead towards the moment of ritual death at the end of the first season.

Everyone knows who Cardan is, and what he's capable of. Jude is the unknown, and that's what makes her interesting. Locke suggesting that they are about to find out what Jude is, foreshadows what she is about to become. Her determination to become untouchable and powerful intensifies the barrier between her and Cardan, because she's unwilling to trust him, or let him in, even knowing he can't lie to her.

Cardan knows Jude can lie, which means he knows that if she did grovel at his feet, it would be a performance at best. All he can have from her is a performance, but he wants her to mean the things she says to him.

Taryn is jealous of the attention Locke is paying Jude. Taryn aspires to gain power through a political match, whereas Jude wants to attain power in her own right. Taryn's jealousy leads to a moment of ritual death in the second season, when she dresses like Jude in order to manipulate Cardan.

Cardan reinforces the barrier by reminding Jude of her place. She is worth less than he is, because he is a Prince of Faerie. The biggest barrier between them (aside from their animosity for each other) is the class difference. Jude is the adopted daughter of a general. Cardan is the Prince of Faerie. Cardan also has to contend with how he is perceived by his friends and family, and caring for a mortal girl would be deemed an embarassment. Unless, of course, that mortal girl could prove her cunning to the whole of Faerie.

Taryn's decision to leave in this scene is symbolic of her choice to abandon Jude. She cannot stand by and watch the decisions Jude is making, so she leaves. She will protect herself instead of Jude, even though Jude would do anything to protect her. It is another way Cardan has isolated Jude, and ensured she feels alone.

Jude's refusal to bow before Cardan's will intrigues him. He is used to people listening to his authority. Jude is determined to create her own authority, and trap Cardan with it. This is a part of the moment of ritual death in the first season, because Cardan allows Jude authority over him. Once he does that, it allows Jude to crown him King of Faerie, and prevent him from escaping his duties the way he had intended.

Her threats to Cardan make him wary of her, especially because she doesn't seem to be afraid of him, even though she should be. She is only a mortal, and making these threats against a Prince of Faerie could be considered treason. Cardan very easily could have her arrested, but he doesn't. A part of the reason is because he enjoys their animosity, and he's also intrigued by Jude and wants to know what she'll do next.

Jude believes Cardan has come for his revenge for her brash words, but she doesn't think another prince will have come to visit her after her display at the tournament. This visit from Prince Dain signals a shift in status for Jude. Though she is still just a mortal, she is offered a role as a spy. Mortals are able to lie, and they are easily overlooked. They make for good assassins and spies. It is the only kind of power anyone would offer Jude, and she will gladly take it, and claw her way up the ranks. Especially as it will allow her some protection from Cardan. She reports to Prince Dain, now, and Cardan can have no impact on her.

Jude's decision to cover for Cardan and not confess his threats against her also indicates her attraction to him. Neither of them is willing to relinquish their animosity towards the other. Their rivalry is theirs, and theirs alone.

This scene acts as a reminder that in this world, only humans can lie. Faeries can speak around the truth, but they cannot tell a lie. They can omit a fact, but they have to be careful in their wording. Jude can lie, and that makes her powerful.

Jude's desire for power could also be interpreted as a desire to be on the same level as Cardan. Especially as she consistently seeks political power. She wants to control the throne of Faerie, and find a way to manipulate the crown itself. She will betray whoever it takes to ensure she is never powerless again, and Cardan would allow Jude to manipulate him just to see what she does.

The rules of enchantments are very important, because they allow for the confines of the magic system. There are ways around the resistance of enchantment, but the resistance acts as a safeguard, a way to defend oneself. Jude wants something more permanent, so she can protect herself from Cardan. She doesn't want him to ever have control of her.

The dismissive way Prince Dain speaks of Cardan foreshadows the way Cardan was neglected as a child. Later in season one, Jude will infiltrate Cardan's home and learn what his home life is like. Realising the kind of harsh punishments he faces from his older brother Balekin, helps her to understand why Cardan acts the way he does. If he isn't cruel, he is punished for his kindness. It helps Jude begin to overcome the barriers between them, because she realises that he was raised to be cruel, and he fights it when he can. He is simply not always in a position where resistance is possible. In a way, he envies Jude for her freedom. As she is mortal, no one has any expectations for what she will do. Cardan cannot escape the expectations placed on him, and when his family remembers to care about him, they have expectations of the kind of person he will be.

This is the kind of power Jude has been waiting for. This is the way she can prove herself to Cardan. She can become powerful in her own right, without requiring the support of Madoc, or needing to marry into a powerful position. She has always wanted to earn power that no one could take away from her.

The offer of a Geis is incredibly powerful. It will mean no one can enchant Jude. It is a measure of protection that is completely permanent. Even if someone stripped her of her protective measures, she would still be safe from glamour and enchantment. It allows her a measure of control she never would have had otherwise, and it means Cardan's magic can't touch her. In terms of power, it places them on the same playing field.

It is an offer of servitude. Jude is still limited in her powers, for as long as Prince Dain may live. However, it is much more of a protection than she has had previously. It makes her feel more powerful knowing that Cardan cannot use his magic to control her, and he will not know she cannot be controlled.
